# Agent-Based Epidemic Model (ABM) An educational, agent-based simulation of epidemic spread built in R, where each agent progresses through a stochastic disease-state pathway while interacting through a configurable social network. Developed for **Mathematical Modeling and Simulation**. > **Attribution:** The core modeling code in this repository is adapted from Shane T. Mueller's research work on modeling psychological impacts on epidemic spread.

--- ## Table of Contents - [Overview](#-overview) - [Why Agent-Based Modeling?](#-why-agent-based-modeling) - [Model Architecture](#-model-architecture) - [Disease State Machine](#-disease-state-machine) - [Simulation Workflow](#-simulation-workflow) - [Getting Started](#-getting-started) - [Usage](#-usage) - [Key Parameters](#-key-parameters) - [Repository Structure](#-repository-structure) - [Example Scenarios](#-example-scenarios) - [Sample Outputs](#-sample-outputs) - [Limitations](#-limitations) - [Related Simulations](#-related-simulations) - [Contributing](#-contributing) - [License](#-license) - [Citation & Attribution](#-citation--attribution) --- ## Overview This project implements a **discrete-time, agent-based model (ABM)** of infectious disease spread, built step-by-step in an R Markdown notebook (`1b__ABM_epidemic-model-base.Rmd`). Rather than relying on aggregate compartmental equations (like a classic SIR model), the simulation tracks **individual agents**, each with: - A **biological state** (7 possible disease stages, from unexposed to death) - A **psychological state** (a placeholder for future work on compliance, belief, and behavior) - A position in a **social network** that governs who they interact with each day Because interactions happen over an explicit network rather than a fully-mixed population, the model can capture clustering, superspreading, and the effects of policy interventions (e.g., stay-at-home orders) in ways that classic compartmental models cannot. ## Why Agent-Based Modeling? | Compartmental (SIR) Models | This Agent-Based Model | |---|---| | Assumes homogeneous mixing | Interactions follow an explicit social network | | Tracks population-level counts | Tracks individual-level state per agent | | Hard to represent heterogeneous behavior | Naturally supports per-agent attributes (age, psychology, compliance) | | Policy changes are applied globally to rate constants | Policy changes can be applied per-agent, per-day, or per-network-tie | | Fast, closed-form intuition | Slower, but reveals emergent effects (clustering, rebound waves) | ## Model Architecture

The codebase is organized around four cooperating components: 1. **Agent layer** — `makeAgent()` constructs a list-based agent object holding psychological state, biological state, age, the next scheduled biological state, and a countdown timer. 2. **Disease progression engine** — a transition matrix (`bioTransition`) plus per-state minimum/maximum duration vectors (`bioMin`, `bioMax`) fully specify the stochastic disease pathway. `setAgentState()`, `updateAgent()`, and `transitionAgent()` drive an agent through this pathway one simulated day at a time. 3. **Social network generator** — `makeNetwork()` builds a contact network from one or more preferential-attachment (small-world-like) graphs, optionally densified by connecting N-step neighbors, to emulate realistic "clumpy" real-world social structure (e.g., a tight-knit club vs. a large lecture class). 4. **Simulation engine** — the daily loop samples contacts from the network, applies a contagion probability to each contact between an infectious and a susceptible agent, advances every agent's countdown/state, and logs the population-wide state distribution (`disthistory`) for later plotting. ## Disease State Machine The biological model defines **7 discrete states**, encoded as a directed, weighted transition graph (`bioTransition`), with stage durations drawn from a **Uniform(bioMin, bioMax)** distribution set at the moment an agent enters that state ("ballistic" scheduling, rather than a memoryless exponential/geometric process): | # | State | Description | |---|---|---| | 1 | Unexposed | Susceptible; has not contracted the disease | | 2 | Asymptomatic & contagious | Infected, no symptoms yet, can transmit | | 3 | Symptomatic & contagious | Showing symptoms, can transmit | | 4 | Symptomatic & not contagious | Showing symptoms, no longer transmits | | 5 | Post-COVID immune | Recovered, immune | | 6 | Naturally immune | Immune from the start of the simulation | | 7 | Death | Absorbing state | See the [full transition diagram](assets/disease-state-diagram.svg) above for branch probabilities (e.g., a symptomatic-contagious agent has a 55% chance of recovering vs. a 45% chance of death in the base configuration — tune these to match your scenario). ## Simulation Workflow

Each simulated day, the model: 1. **Initializes** (once) the agent pool and social network, seeding a handful of index infections. 2. **Samples contacts** for every agent from their position in the social network (with a tunable probability of instead contacting a random stranger). 3. **Transmits** the disease across each sampled contact pair according to `contagionProb`, only when one party is infectious and the other is susceptible. 4. **Updates** every agent's countdown and transitions any agent whose timer has expired. 5. **Records** the population-wide count in each biological state for that day. This loop repeats for `numDays`, and key parameters (`numInteractions`, `contagionProb`, `sampleFromNetwork`) can be specified as **per-day vectors**, enabling policy experiments such as a stay-at-home order that is imposed on one day and lifted on another. ## Getting Started ### Prerequisites - **R** ≥ 4.0 - **RStudio** (recommended, for rendering the `.Rmd`) - The following R packages: ```r install.packages(c( "ggplot2", "dplyr", "sna", "knitr", "reshape2", "igraph", "gridExtra", "rmdformats" )) ``` ### Clone the repository ```bash git clone https://github.com//.git cd ``` ### Render the notebook Open `1b__ABM_epidemic-model-base.Rmd` in RStudio and click **Knit**, or run from the console: ```r rmarkdown::render("1b__ABM_epidemic-model-base.Rmd") ``` ## Usage The notebook is organized as a progressive tutorial — each section builds on the last, so it is best read (or knit) top to bottom the first time. Once you're comfortable with the mechanics, the core simulation block can be re-parameterized and re-run directly: ```r set.seed(100) numAgents <- 500 naturalImmunity <- .01 # proportion immune at t = 0 numInteractions <- 10 # average contacts per agent per day numDays <- 50 contagionProb <- .1 # transmission probability per risky contact socialnetwork <- makeNetwork(numAgents, numsets = 1, power = .5, steps = 2) # ... seed infections, then run the daily loop (see notebook for full code) ``` To model a **policy intervention** (e.g., a temporary stay-at-home order), pass per-day vectors instead of scalars: ```r numInteractions <- rep(10, numDays) numInteractions[10:numDays] <- 3 # restrictions begin on day 10 numInteractions[25:numDays] <- 10 # restrictions lifted on day 25 ``` ## Key Parameters | Parameter | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | `numAgents` | integer | Population size (recommended ≤ ~1000 for reasonable runtime) | | `naturalImmunity` | 0–1 | Fraction of agents immune at simulation start | | `numInteractions` | integer or per-day vector | Average number of contacts per agent per day | | `numDays` | integer | Simulation horizon | | `contagionProb` | 0–1 or per-day vector | Probability of transmission on an infectious–susceptible contact | | `sampleFromNetwork` | 0–1 or per-day vector | Probability a contact is drawn from the agent's network vs. a random stranger | | `bioMin` / `bioMax` | vectors | Min/max duration (days) for each biological state | | `bioTransition` | matrix | Branch probabilities between biological states | ## Repository Structure ``` . ├── 1b__ABM_epidemic-model-base.Rmd # Main tutorial notebook (this model) ├── assets/ # Diagrams used in this README │ ├── disease-state-diagram.svg │ ├── simulation-workflow.svg │ └── architecture-overview.svg ├── README.md └── (companion notebooks referenced below, if included in this repo) ├── epidemic-demographics.Rmd ├── epidemic-michigan.Rmd └── epidemic-travellers.Rmd ``` ## Example Scenarios The notebook walks through three progressively more realistic simulations: | Scenario | Network assumption | Behavior once symptomatic | Notable outcome | |---|---|---|---| | **Fully-mixed population** | Everyone can contact everyone | No behavior change | ~75% of the population infected by day ~25; single fast peak | | **Social network, limited symptomatic contact** | Preferential-attachment network | Symptomatic agents quarantine | Slower, network-shaped spread | | **Social network + policy shock** | Preferential-attachment network | Interactions cut from day 10–25 (stay-at-home) | Two distinct waves — initial rise, then a rebound after restrictions lift | ## Sample Outputs The notebook produces, for each scenario: - A **stacked area / bar chart** of the population's daily distribution across all 7 biological states - A simplified **SIR-style line chart** (susceptible / infected / recovered) - A **daily new-case bar chart** ("flatten the curve" view) - Optional **network visualizations** colored by current disease state, frame-by-frame per day > Tip: after knitting the notebook, drop a couple of your favorite generated plots into `assets/` (e.g. `assets/sample-sir-plot.png`) and reference them here with `![SIR plot](assets/sample-sir-plot.png)` so the README shows real results from your run. ## Limitations - This is a **teaching model**, not a validated epidemiological forecasting tool — do not use it to make real-world predictions. - Runtime scales with `numAgents × numInteractions × numDays`; simulations much beyond ~1,000 agents become slow in base R. - The psychological-state dimension is currently a placeholder (`psychstate`) — expanding it (distancing, compliance, belief in misinformation) is a suggested extension. - Disease parameters (transition probabilities, stage durations) are illustrative, not calibrated to any specific real pathogen. ## Related Simulations This base model is extended in three companion student projects exploring: - **Demographic networks** — school, workplace, and family sub-networks - **Geography** — a spatially-explicit model of the state of Michigan - **Travelers** — the effect of vacationers/travelers reintroducing the disease into a population ## Contributing Contributions, extensions, and classroom adaptations are welcome: 1. Fork the repository 2. Create a feature branch (`git checkout -b feature/psych-states`) 3. Commit your changes with clear messages 4. Open a pull request describing the extension or fix Ideas for contributions: richer psychological-state modeling, age-stratified risk, hospital-capacity constraints, vaccination rollout, calibration to real epidemiological data. ## License Specify your preferred license here (e.g., MIT, CC-BY-4.0). If this is coursework, check with your instructor before adding an open-source license. ## Citation & Attribution - Core agent/disease/network modeling code adapted from **Shane T. Mueller**'s research on psychological impacts on epidemic spread. - Notebook developed for **Mathematical Modeling and Simulation**. If you use or extend this model academically, please retain the attribution above and cite this repository.
